description:

Amidst the bustling streets of Victorian England, Philip's dreams of success clash with the intoxicating allure of love, forcing him to navigate a treacherous landscape of financial intrigue and personal sacrifice. Doyle paints a vivid portrait of a society teetering on the edge of change, where the pursuit of money can lead to unexpected consequences. The central conflict unfolds as Philip grapples with his feelings for his enchanting muse and the demands of a world obsessed with wealth.

With each twist and turn, 'Beyond the City' invites you to question what truly matters: the pursuit of love or the quest for prosperity? title: How to Identify a Real Natural Emerald S
author: durgesh sharma
description:
How to Identify a Real Natural Emerald Stone
Emeralds are admired for their rich green colour and rarity. Yet not every green stone sold as an emerald is genuine, and genuine stones vary in quality. Before buying, learn a few practical checks and ask clear questions. The safest approach combines visual inspection, gemological testing and reliable documentation. No home test can prove that a stone is natural.
What Is a Natural Emerald?
Emerald is the green variety of the mineral beryl. Its colour comes mainly from trace chromium, vanadium or both. A natural emerald stone forms in the Earth, not in a laboratory. Natural emeralds commonly contain inclusions: tiny crystals, threads, clouds or garden-like patterns known as a jardin.
Inclusions do not prove authenticity. Imitations and laboratory-grown emeralds can also contain features that look convincing. Treat appearance as a clue, not a verdict.
7 Ways to Check an Emerald Before Buying
1. Examine the Colour
A genuine emerald is usually green to bluish-green. Colour varies with origin, trace elements, cutting and treatment. An unusually uniform, vivid colour at a very low price deserves scrutiny. However, colour alone cannot distinguish natural emerald from synthetic material or imitation.
2. Look for Inclusions With a Loupe
Inspect the stone with a 10x jeweller’s loupe. Natural emeralds often contain crystals, fractures or liquid-filled features, sometimes in irregular patterns. But not every natural emerald has obvious inclusions, and laboratory-grown stones may contain them too. Never use inclusions as sole proof.
3. Check for Bubbles
Round gas bubbles are common in glass imitations. If you see obvious bubbles, ask a gemologist to examine the stone. Do not judge by one feature: inclusions can be complex, and a phone photograph cannot replace microscopic examination.
4. Ask Whether the Stone Has Been Treated
Many emeralds are clarity-enhanced with oil or resin to make fractures less visible. This accepted trade practice can affect value and care. Ask whether the stone is untreated, oiled, resin-filled or otherwise treated. The seller should disclose this clearly.
5. Request an Independent Gem Laboratory Report
For a valuable purchase, request a report from a recognised independent gem laboratory. It should identify the material as natural emerald, note detected treatments where possible and include details matching the stone. Verify the report number with the laboratory when possible. A seller’s certificate is not necessarily independent.
6. Compare Weight, Measurements and Price
Check the carat weight and dimensions in millimetres against the listing and report. Price depends on colour, transparency, clarity, cut, weight, origin and treatment. A low price for a large, vivid, clean stone may be a warning, but a high price does not prove authenticity. Compare stones with similar characteristics.
7. Buy From a Seller Who Answers Questions
Choose a seller who provides product details, treatment disclosure, a return policy and documentation. Ask whether an advertised origin is supported by a laboratory opinion. Avoid pressure to buy immediately or promises of guaranteed powers or investment returns. Keep the invoice and report.
Before inspecting a stone, ask whether the description refers to natural emerald, laboratory-grown emerald or an imitation. Also ask whether the price includes a report and whether the report describes treatment. If the seller cannot answer basic questions, pause the purchase. A reputable seller should welcome reasonable checks and give you time to review the details. Remember that origin claims, such as Colombian or Zambian, may require specialist testing and should not be assumed from colour. These questions help you compare stones fairly and make a decision based on evidence rather than sales language and disclosure.
Natural, Synthetic and Imitation Emerald: Know the Difference
A natural emerald forms in the Earth. A laboratory-grown, or synthetic, emerald has essentially the same chemical composition and crystal structure, but is created in controlled conditions. It is emerald, but not natural. An imitation is another material made to look similar, such as green glass, dyed quartz or another green gem.
These categories can look alike to an untrained eye. A gemologist uses magnification and, when needed, instruments that examine optical and physical properties. Ask sellers to use precise terms: “created,” “simulated” and “natural” are not interchangeable.
Can You Identify a Real Emerald at Home?
You can screen for warning signs, but cannot reliably confirm natural origin at home. Avoid scratch tests, heating, chemicals or tapping; they are unreliable and may damage the gem. Colour, bubbles and inclusions offer clues, not proof. For a significant purchase, make the sale conditional on an independent report and reasonable return period.
Why Certification and a Gemstone Recommendation Matter
A sound purchase considers authenticity, treatment, quality, intended use and price. A gemstone recommendation can help narrow choices by budget and preference, but cannot replace verification. If buying for astrological reasons, regard spiritual claims as beliefs, not proven benefits, and still check identity and treatment.
Frequently Asked Questions
1. How can I tell if an emerald is natural?
Visual features can provide clues, but only suitable gemological testing can reliably separate natural emerald from laboratory-grown or imitation material. Request an independent report for confidence.
2. Do real emeralds have bubbles?
Natural emeralds may contain inclusions, but obvious round gas bubbles are more commonly associated with glass. A gemologist should assess the feature under magnification before drawing a conclusion.
3. Are all natural emeralds treated?
No. Some are untreated, while many receive clarity enhancement, often with oil or resin. Ask the seller to disclose the treatment and have it recorded where possible.
4. Is a lab-grown emerald a real emerald?
It is emerald material with essentially the same chemical composition and crystal structure, but it is grown in a laboratory rather than formed naturally. It should be sold clearly as laboratory-grown.
5. Should I buy an emerald without a certificate?
For an inexpensive item, your decision may depend on the seller’s return policy and disclosures. For a valuable stone, an independent laboratory report is strongly recommended.

title: Lyric before the take
author: Jordan Vale
description:
This show is a working notebook for lyric writers and small audio teams who need a full sung demo before they open a DAW.

The stall I keep running into is not the mix. It is the first listen: does the refrain carry, do the adjectives in the brief still hold, and would another engine take the same words somewhere more usable? Locking into one generative model too early often means polishing the wrong take.

On each episode I walk a short fragment from notebook to first listen. The online studio I use for that pass is Doremi—create-music can run the same lyrics or one-line idea across the models listed on the product (Suno, Lyria, YuE2, Mureka, ElevenLabs, and MiniMax) so several takes stay comparable while the brief stays fixed. After listening, extend, cover, remix, mashup, and section replace adjust one stretch without regenerating the whole draft.

Commercial-license certificates follow Doremi’s public rules: available with an active annual plan or after buying a credit pack, not with free or monthly-only accounts. Songs based on imported audio sit outside that certificate path.

This feed is process notes, not a label roster and not a substitute for live capture when a brief needs only human performance. Limits stated once: Doremi drafts demos; it does not replace a finished production session.

Sometimes I'll share my own thoughts and experiences. Other times, I'll invite people to sit down and talk about theirs. We may agree, disagree, laugh, reflect, or leave a conversation with more questions than we started with.

No perfect people. No perfect conversations. No perfect answers. Just life, as we experience it.

title: Room for Change | For Therapists, Counsellors & Psychologists
author: Leah King (clinical social worker and psychotherapist) & Alexia Leachman
description:
If you're a therapist, you've probably sat with a client who has come to understand, logically, why they react the way they do. They still respond in the way they learned to keep themselves safe, and neither of you has figured out why it's still happening.

The rapport is good and the insight is there, but the reflex response to certain situations is still sneakily waiting to burst into the room. The feeling of breakthrough is tangible, for you and for your client. You just need to figure out how to crack the code!

Room for Change is a podcast for therapists, counsellors and psychotherapists about this experience.

Leah King is a clinical social worker and psychotherapist with more than ten years in practice. She trained in EMDR, then came across Head Trash Clearance and started using it with her clients. Alexia Leachman developed Head Trash Clearance and has been using it in a therapeutic setting for more than fifteen years. Leah uses it as a therapist. Alexia uses it for therapeutic work. That's the common ground these conversations come from.

Together they talk about using Head Trash Clearance with clients on this threshold: what it is, how to bring it into play with the work you already do as a therapist, and what can unlock when you have the key to breaking the repeating patterns your client longs to live without.

Some of what we get into:

- working gently with heavy material, so a client can go near it without being flooded
- clearing what a session leaves in your own body
- what happens when a client changes and the people around them don't
- using the same method on yourself that you use with your clients

You can find out more about the Head Trash Clearance method, and the training for therapists, at headtrashclearance.com.

*A Note About the Name of Our Savior*
Throughout history and across languages, our Savior has been known by different names, including *Jesus Christ* , *Yeshua* , *Yehoshua* , *Yahushua* , and *Yahushua HaMashiach* (“the Messiah”). Out of reverence, we recognize that He is far more than a name. He is the Son of God, the Messiah, our Redeemer, Savior, and King. title: Science Unwound
author: Alan Best
description:
Your most vivid memory might be a lie.

Welcome to the very first episode of Science Unwound, where we take the science that runs your life and unwind it, one thread at a time. Host Alan Best opens the show, and Rachel and Harry go inside the most complicated object in the known universe, the human brain, to ask a simple question: how do we remember?

In this episode:

  • Why memory isn't a filing cabinet, and the 100-year hunt for the "engram," the physical trace a memory leaves in the brain
  • The three stages of memory, and why an all-nighter before a test works against you
  • Henry Molaison, "Patient H.M.," who lost the ability to form new memories after surgery in 1953 and became the most important patient in the history of neuroscience
  • Short-term, long-term, explicit and implicit memory, and how they work together
  • Flashbulb memories, Elizabeth Loftus's false-memory experiments, and what they mean for eyewitness testimony
  • Why your brain rebuilds every memory each time you recall it
  • The forgetting curve, and science-backed ways to remember better

Sources:

  • Lashley, K. S. (1950). In search of the engram. Symposia of the Society for Experimental Biology, 4.
  • Liu, X., Ramirez, S., Tonegawa, S. et al. (2012). Optogenetic stimulation of a hippocampal engram activates fear memory recall. Nature, 484.
  • Wilson, M. A. & McNaughton, B. L. (1994). Reactivation of hippocampal ensemble memories during sleep. Science, 265.
  • Walker, M. P. & Stickgold, R. (2006). Sleep, memory, and plasticity. Annual Review of Psychology, 57.
  • Scoville, W. B. & Milner, B. (1957). Loss of recent memory after bilateral hippocampal lesions. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery and Psychiatry, 20.
  • Corkin, S. (2013). Permanent Present Tense: The Unforgettable Life of the Amnesic Patient, H.M. Basic Books.
  • Miller, G. A. (1956). The magical number seven, plus or minus two. Psychological Review, 63.
  • Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24.
  • Neisser, U. & Harsch, N. (1992). Phantom flashbulbs: False recollections of hearing the news about Challenger.
  • Talarico, J. M. & Rubin, D. C. (2003). Confidence, not consistency, characterizes flashbulb memories. Psychological Science, 14.
  • Loftus, E. F. & Palmer, J. C. (1974). Reconstruction of automobile destruction. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 13.
  • Loftus, E. F. & Pickrell, J. E. (1995). The formation of false memories. Psychiatric Annals, 25.
  • Shaw, J. & Porter, S. (2015). Constructing rich false memories of committing crime. Psychological Science, 26.
  • Innocence Project, Eyewitness Identification Reform (innocenceproject.org).
  • Bartlett, F. C. (1932). Remembering: A Study in Experimental and Social Psychology. Cambridge University Press.
  • Nader, K., Schafe, G. E. & LeDoux, J. E. (2000). Fear memories require protein synthesis in the amygdala for reconsolidation after retrieval. Nature, 406.
  • Ebbinghaus, H. (1885). Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology.
  • Roediger, H. L. & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning. Psychological Science, 17.
  • Erickson, K. I. et al. (2011). Exercise training increases size of hippocampus and improves memory. PNAS, 108.
  • Luria, A. R. (1968). The Mind of a Mnemonist. Basic Books.

title: The Toy Box Killer

Behind the Locked Door: The Toy Box Killer
The Toy Box Killer is one of the most disturbing criminal cases in American history. This two-part true crime documentary explores the crimes of David Parker Ray, a convicted kidnapper and torturer who became known as the Toy Box Killer. Operating in New Mexico, Ray used an isolated trailer that he called his personal torture chamber. Behind its ordinary appearance was a carefully prepared environment designed to imprison, terrorize, and abuse his victims.

This podcast examines how Ray carried out his crimes, how his methods helped him maintain control, and how investigators eventually uncovered the horrifying truth. It also explores the role of his accomplices, the importance of survivor testimony, and the investigation that brought the case into public attention.

Beyond the shocking details, this series focuses on the human consequences of violent crime, the courage of survivors, and the challenges faced by investigators when victims cannot easily identify or remember their attackers.

Through two episodes, listeners will discover how an apparently ordinary individual concealed a deeply disturbing criminal life, how one survivor's escape helped expose his activities, and why this case remains an important reminder of the need to listen to victims and pursue justice.

50-hour Yin Yoga Teacher Training
100-hour Yin Yoga Teacher Training

Feeling like you've got more to give...
Something that no-one really talks about.

For the guys who aren't massively out of shape, unfit, or underperforming. 
The guys who from the outside, are doing well...

Because I believe fitness is the key that unlocks the door to the life you want.

Passionate erotic stories that take their time, and then don’t.

What’s the Issue? is a podcast series from the Office of the Police and Crime Commissioner for Dyfed-Powys, exploring the issues affecting policing, justice and community safety across the Dyfed-Powys area.  Hosted by Police and Crime Commissioner Dafydd Llywelyn, each episode features conversations with experts and partners.

title: What We Make of It
author: Lorenzo Castillo-Rios
description:
We all have our own stories to tell. They come from the chances we take, the people we show up for, and the things we do because they matter to us. That’s the stuff we live for.


What We Make of It is about those stories and the different ways we see them. We get into what we’ve tried, what’s surprised us, and what we’re still figuring out. Some stories start with a decision made. Others start with something no one ever saw coming. Either way, we get a say in what our lives become.

author: Juntrax
description:
A Juntrax Podcast on How Firms Operate Before Automation.
Every week, we sit down with owners, COOs, and HR leaders of professional-services firms to talk about how they really run and grow.
That means how work gets scoped, staffed, tracked, and billed when people, projects, and finances live in spreadsheets and disconnected tools. Our guests share what works, what doesn't, and what they would do differently, long before any software decision gets made. Expect practical, candid conversations you can apply to a firm of 20 to 150 people.

title: Play it or Break it

description: Welcome to Play It or Break It, the music podcast where Brad, Mark, and MTD (Music Torture Dad) put their musical tastes, friendships, and credibility on the line.  From legendary albums and forgotten classics to one-hit wonders and songs that should've never left the recording studio, we're diving into the music that shaped generations — and some that probably should've been left behind.  Expect hilarious debates, unpopular opinions, ridiculous rankings, music trivia, and absolutely no guarantee that anyone knows what they're talking about. No artist is untouchable, no genre is safe, and just because a song sold a million copies doesn't mean we won't tear it apart.  Whether you're a music nerd, a casual listener, or someone who still thinks their favorite band is criminally underrated, pull up a chair and turn up the volume.  Three guys. Too many opinions. One ultimate question:  Do we play it… or break it?

Are shorts ever acceptable in the office? How do you address a peer, a bishop or an ambassador? They answer with wit, history and plenty of practical advice.

In our regular "Debrett's Will Know" segment, Rupert puts your questions to Hugo before he's had a chance to look them up. Topics range from forms of address and titles to dress codes and dinner-party dilemmas.

Good manners aren't about rules for their own sake. They're about care and consideration for others, and On Good Form is here to help you get them right.

description:
Faulkners Surveyors specialises in party wall matters connected with residential building and renovation projects. The service is designed for property owners who need to understand their responsibilities before carrying out work on or near a shared wall, boundary or neighbouring property.

The team provides guidance throughout the party wall process, from understanding whether a project requires a notice through to surveying requirements, Schedule of Condition and Party Wall Awards where applicable.

Typical projects can include loft conversions, extensions, chimney breast removal, alterations to party walls, boundary-related work and excavations close to neighbouring structures.

Faulkners places emphasis on straightforward communication and practical advice. Rather than making party wall procedures unnecessarily complicated, the team explains the relevant process clearly so property owners can make informed decisions about their projects.

The service is intended to support both building owners and adjoining owners, helping clarify rights, responsibilities and the steps involved when construction work could affect neighbouring property.

The Tangent Table. Where the conversation has no map, the detours are the best part, and we don't know where this is going either.
